title: Prototype and Object Pool
idea: Prototype makes new objects by cloning a configured one. Object Pool keeps expensive objects alive and lends them out, so you reuse instead of rebuilding.
points: A prototype object owns a `clone()` method that knows how deep to copy.
Clone a preset, then change only the fields that differ.
A pool hands out a free object, or creates one while under its limit.
Released objects return to the free list; a full pool refuses or waits.

steps.caption: The pool starts empty. It creates connections lazily, up to a maximum of two.
First `acquire()`: nothing is free, so the pool creates `conn 1` and lends it.
Second `acquire()`: still under the limit, so it creates `conn 2`.
Third `acquire()`: nothing free and the limit is reached, so the pool throws.
`release(conn 1)` moves it back to the free list. It is not destroyed.
The next `acquire()` reuses `conn 1`. No new connection is built.

code.title: Prototype with clone()
code.caption: `clone()` copies the tags array; a plain shallow copy shares it. `structuredClone` copies data but drops the class.

walk.text: `clone()` decides the depth: a new array, so tags are not shared.
Clone a preset and change only what differs. The preset stays intact.
`Object.assign` copies the array reference, so pushing edits the preset too.
`clone()` keeps the class; `structuredClone` returns a plain object.

code.title: A bounded Object Pool
code.caption: Change the limit to 3 and run again: the third `acquire()` now succeeds.

walk.text: Free list, a set of lent objects, and a count of how many exist.
Reuse a free object first; create one only while under `max`.
Full pool: fail loudly. Real pools often queue the caller instead.
Only objects this pool lent can return, so a double release is ignored.
After a release, `acquire()` hands back the very same object.

pitfalls: A shallow copy shares nested arrays and objects; clone those explicitly.
Reset a pooled object's state on release, or the next caller sees old data.
Pool only objects that are costly to create; pooling cheap objects adds bugs, not speed.

quiz.why: Spread copies top-level fields, so `name` is separate. `opts` is one shared object, so the change shows through `base`.

takeaway: Clone presets with care; pool only what is expensive to build.
